source.title: Two Minds Better Than One: Collaborative Reward Modeling for LLM Alignment
source.authors: Jiazheng Zhang; Wenqing Jing; Zizhuo Zhang; Zhiheng Xi; Shihan Dou; Rongxiang Weng; Jiahuan Li; Jingang Wang; Mingxu Chai; Shibo Hong; Yuming Yang; Chenhao Huang; Tao Gui; Qi Zhang; Xuanjing Huang

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper, including appendices. It has minor extraction artifacts, but no apparent cut-off affecting the relevant results.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out preference accuracy of LLM reward models under synthetic preference-label noise, extending generalization analysis to preference modeling. It does not test the specific conditions or properties in V1–V8.
record.gate_note: The paper reports held-out preference accuracy under different training noise levels and reports reward-model generalization to RewardBench. These results concern generalization, but do not measure training-to-test error gaps or the specific interventions and properties named in V1–V8. Baseline comparisons and the CRM method’s results are included where they directly report held-out accuracy.
record.test_reason: The study measures reward-model accuracy under preference-label noise and evaluates its CRM method. None of its results tests V1–V8. Partial label corruption does not establish random-label memorization alongside natural-label generalization (V1), and loss-based preference filtering does not identify memorized examples by their inclusion influence or compare their removal with random removal (V8).
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that CRM improves reward-model generalization through peer review and curriculum learning, improves downstream alignment in their experiments, and extends to DPO.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains LLM reward models on human preference pairs, including synthetically corrupted labels, and evaluates held-out preference accuracy; it does not use the original methods or measures in V1–V8.
record.method_sensitivity: Training preference-noise level and evaluation dataset (in-domain sets versus RewardBench OOD) change reported accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: For standard RMs trained on HH-RLHF, RewardBench accuracy decreases from 66.53% to 65.78% to 64.42% under 0%, 20%, and 40% injected preference flips. CRM achieves 77.63%, 76.19%, and 74.36%, respectively.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Injected preference-label noise can reduce held-out reward-model accuracy, and collaborative preference filtering with curriculum learning can improve accuracy in the tested settings.

record.problems: The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the extracted accuracy values. Its reward-model experiments use a stated 3B base model, and the paper notes computational limits on model scale. These measurements do not provide training error or a train–test gap.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 and Appendix D report additional methods, datasets, and ID/OOD evaluations. Those were omitted to keep the extraction focused on the reported Standard RM and CRM held-out RewardBench results under HH-RLHF noise conditions; no rows were omitted for any tested claim version because none was tested.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fitting of fixed random labels, natural-label held-out accuracy under the same recipe, and chance-level held-out accuracy with random labels.
Width-dependent test error beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizers under specified tuning budgets and recovery interventions.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and changes to training recipes.
Dropout effects, underfitting, training-set size, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness, generalization gaps, and ranking against alternative measures.
Influence-defined memorization and test-accuracy effects of removing memorized versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The absence of a training–test gap is not itself grounds for exclusion; the measured interventions do not match any version. Excerpt E1's 83.85% to 60.60% decline concerns Skywork-Reward, not the HH-RLHF rows R1–R3. The paper also reports larger backbones in Figure 5 despite its limitations paragraph emphasizing a 3B base model.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization versus natural-label generalization; specified architectures and training recipes.
Network-width sweep beyond interpolation and test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and architectural bias.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizers and their held-out performance.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout and weight-decay effects on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to the training–test gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.
